shape.name: Shape E - Receptive Skills (Traditional)
shape.description: Traditional receptive skills lesson focusing on practising listening sub-skills, with a post-listening discussion that recycles the content into a productive speaking task.
shape.pedagogical_justification: The lesson opens with a listening dictation that activates the question forms students will hear in the main text, then practises listening for specific information and detailed comprehension in a radio interview. The final stage recycles the interview content into a structured speed-dating discussion about climate change, moving learners from receptive to productive use.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practised listening for [specific information/detail] in the context of [topic], and will have discussed [topic] using [structure].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will have practised listening for specific information and detailed comprehension in a radio interview about a flood at the China-Nepal border, and will have discussed flood risk and climate change using a five-step speaking structure.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
5 September, 2026
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
E (Receptive Skills - Listening)
Materials:
Slideshow, audio interview, dictation tape, speaking cue cards
Assessment:
Dictation, listening tasks, discussion observation
Skills:
Listening, Speaking

stages.stage_aim: To set the context and activate background knowledge about floods
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: Where is this? What do you see? Let students speculate in pairs.
Advance to the title slide: The flood at the China-Nepal border. Confirm the theme.
Ask: Have you ever seen a flood? What happens when a river floods?

stages.stage_aim: To raise the importance of the topic and connect it to students' own context
procedure: Show the 'Why is this lesson important?' slide.
Read the three points aloud. Emphasise: floods are a real risk across Asia, including Thailand.
Tell students: today you will listen to a radio interview about this flood, then discuss climate change.

stages.stage: Dictation - listen and write the questions
stages.stage_aim: To practise listening for specific information by writing dictated questions
procedure: Show the dictation slide. Explain: you will hear eight questions, each read twice. Write each one exactly.
Play the dictation tape (questions.mp3). Students write the eight questions.
Display the 'Check your dictation' slides, Parts 1-4. Read each question aloud; students tick or correct what they wrote.

stages.stage_aim: To listen for detailed comprehension in a radio interview
procedure: Introduce the interview: journalist Lucy Milligan interviews aid worker Emma McKinley.
Play Part 1 twice. Students answer questions 1-2. Check on the 'Answers - Part 1' slide.
Play Part 2 twice. Students answer questions 3-4. Check on the 'Answers - Part 2' slide.
Play Part 3 twice. Students answer questions 5-6. Check on the 'Answers - Part 3' slide.
Play Part 4 twice. Students answer questions 7-8. Check on the 'Answers - Part 4' slide.

stages.stage: Speaking - model card and speed dating
stages.stage_aim: To discuss flood risk and climate change using a five-step speaking structure
procedure: Show the model speaking card. Walk through the five steps: Open, Opinion, Reason, Agree/disagree, Agreement.
Model one short example with a student.
Speed dating Set A (structured cards with language support). Two-minute rounds; rotate partners.
Speed dating Set B (bare cards, no language support). Two-minute rounds; rotate partners.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate the lesson and give feedback on the discussion
procedure: Ask groups: What did you agree on? Elicit a few conclusions.
Give content feedback first, then language feedback on the discussion language.
Quick recap: What was the most surprising fact you heard today?

metadata.topic: The flood at the China-Nepal border - listening and discussion
materials: Audio interview: 'World Stories' - Lucy Milligan interviews aid worker Emma McKinley (four parts, played twice)
Slideshow: The Flood at the China-Nepal Border
Audio: Dictation tape (eight questions, each read twice)
Speaking cue cards: climate change discussion - Set A (structured) and Set B (bare)
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will have practised listening for specific information and detailed comprehension in a radio interview about a flood at the China-Nepal border, and will have discussed flood risk and climate change using a five-step speaking structure.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: Learners will also have practised listening to and writing dictated questions, and will use opinion, reason, agreement and compromise language to reach a shared position in a speed-dating discussion.
answer_key: Dictation - the eight questions
1. Emma says the flood was not a normal flood. What was it like, and why was it so dangerous?
2. Why was the loud noise so surprising to the people in Nuwakot?
3. Why did so many people first believe that there had been an earthquake?
4. Why is it so hard for scientists to warn people before a glacier collapses?
5. Give two examples of the damage that the flood caused to buildings and infrastructure.
6. How many people were affected in total, and around how many children lost their classrooms?
7. Emma says the danger is not over. Why?
8. Why does Emma think that this is a climate story, and not only a Nepal story?
Interview Part 1 - Questions 1-2
1. The flood was a solid wall of water, mud, rocks and broken ice. It moved incredibly fast, so people had no time to run.
2. The noise sounded like thunder, but the sky was clear and blue, with no clouds.
Interview Part 2 - Questions 3-4
3. The US Geological Survey recorded a small tremor, about 4.4, so many people believed an earthquake had caused a landslide.
4. The Himalayas are huge and remote, and there are thousands of glaciers, so scientists cannot say which one will break, or when.
Interview Part 3 - Questions 5-6
5. The flood destroyed homes, roads and bridges, and it blocked the tunnels of hydroelectric power stations.
6. About 65,000 people were affected, and around 10,000 children lost their classrooms.
Interview Part 4 - Questions 7-8
7. A barrier lake has formed behind rocks and debris. Water is building up behind it, and if it breaks, there could be a second flood.
8. The warming planet makes flooding worse across Asia. Thailand is also at risk, and countries like Nepal cause little of the problem but feel it first.
